title: Creating Repositories, Staging & .gitignore
description: Initialize new Git repositories, master file tracking lifecycles with git status and git add, and exclude unwanted files with .gitignore.

blocks.content: When you start a new project or want to add Git to an existing folder, the first thing you do is **initialise a repository**. This creates a hidden `.git` folder where Git stores all the history. You never need to touch that folder directly.

## Starting and Checking Status

Initialise Git in a folder:
```
git init
```

See the current state of your files:
```
git status
```

`git status` tells you three things:
- Which branch you're on
- Which files have changed but aren't staged yet
- Which files are staged and ready to commit

## The Staging Area

The staging area is what makes Git powerful. Instead of saving every file change at once, you choose exactly what goes into the next commit.

```
# Stage one specific file
git add README.md

# Stage all changed files at once
git add .
```

Think of the staging area like a shopping basket. You browse (edit files) and place items in the basket (stage). Only when you check out (commit) does the purchase become permanent.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Edit files"] --> B["git add"]
    B --> C["Staging Area"]
    C --> D["git commit"]
    D --> E["Repository History"]
```

If you stage something by mistake, remove it from staging without losing your changes:
```
git restore --staged filename
```

`git init` turns an ordinary folder into a project Git can watch. `git status` is a dashboard that tells you what has changed and what is ready to save.

Think of staging as putting selected photos into an album before you print it. `git add` selects changes; it does not permanently save them.

blocks.question: You changed two files but only want to commit one of them. What do you do?
options: Delete the file you don't want to commit
Stage only the file you want using `git add filename`
Commit all files and then undo the one you didn't want
Git automatically picks the most recently changed file
blocks.explanation: `git add filename` stages a specific file. Only staged files are included in the next commit. The other file stays in your working directory, unchanged, and you can stage and commit it later.

blocks.prompt: Stage a file called README.md for the next commit.
